theme: 3 terms on repeating work over values

terms.definition: A loop that runs the same code once for each item in a collection or sequence.
terms.example: I used a for-in loop to go through every photo name and print it.

terms.definition: A span of values from a start to an end, written with operators like 1...5 (closed) or 0 up to 5 (half-open).
terms.example: I wrote the loop over a range from one to ten, so it runs exactly ten times.

terms.definition: A function that gives you a sequence of numbers that moves from a start value toward an end value by a step you choose.
terms.example: I used stride to count from zero to one hundred in steps of ten for the progress marks.

quizzes.question: Which function lets you count by a custom step, such as every tenth number?
Which one repeats the same code once for every item in a collection?
Which one is a span of values from a start to an end, like 1...5?

Hi everyone! Today we talk about repeating work in Swift.

Today's 3 terms
for-in Loop - runs the same code once for each item in a collection.
Range - a span of values from a start to an end, like 1...5.
stride - counts from a start to an end by a step you choose.

Every example is read twice, normal speed and then slow, so you can say it out loud with me.

dialogue.title: Coffee break: the download progress bar

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Mina, I am building the download progress bar. I need marks at ten, twenty, thirty, and so on.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nice. Do you want to write each mark by hand?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: No way. That is a hundred lines. I need a loop.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. A for-in loop runs the same code once for each item.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So I write a for-in loop over the marks, and put my drawing code inside.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. And you do not need an index. The for-in loop gives you each item.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: But I have no array of marks. I only have numbers from one to ten.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Then use a range. Write 1...10, and Swift counts for you.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Does the range include ten?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: With three dots, yes. It is a closed range. With 0..<10, ten is not included.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I always forget this. I used a closed range 0...10 last week, and I got eleven marks.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good lesson. Use a half-open range when you count items from zero.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Now my marks must go by ten, not by one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That is a job for stride. It counts from a start value to an end value, by a step you choose.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So stride from zero through one hundred, by ten.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. With stride, use through if you want to include one hundred.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Cool. It gives me eleven marks in a for-in loop.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A for-in loop, a range, and stride. That is most of your daily loops.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: How do I print every photo name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Use a for-in loop over the array.
